title: Amazon EKS
description: Learn Kubernetes fundamentals and run workloads on Amazon EKS with managed control planes, node groups, and Fargate profiles.

data.text: Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (EKS) is a managed Kubernetes service. AWS runs the Kubernetes control plane for you, including the API server, etcd, and scheduler. You manage the worker nodes and deploy applications using standard Kubernetes tools.

Kubernetes (K8s) is an open-source container orchestration platform. It automates deployment, scaling, and management of containerized applications. Key Kubernetes concepts include Pods (the smallest deployable unit), Deployments, Services, and Namespaces.

data.title: Core Kubernetes Objects
items: **Pod** — a group of one or more containers that share storage and network
**Deployment** — manages Pod replicas and ensures the desired state
**Service** — exposes a set of Pods as a network service
**Namespace** — a virtual cluster inside a physical cluster for isolation

data.text: EKS runs the Kubernetes control plane across multiple AZs for high availability. Worker nodes run in your account and connect to the control plane via EKS-managed networking. You can use managed node groups (AWS manages them) or self-managed node groups.

EKS supports AWS Fargate, so you can run Kubernetes Pods on serverless infrastructure without managing EC2 nodes. EKS networking uses VPC CNI, which assigns each Pod an IP address from your VPC. This lets you use VPC security groups and network policies for Pod-level security.

IAM Roles for Service Accounts (IRSA) lets you associate an IAM role with a Kubernetes service account. Pods using that service account get the IAM role's permissions. This is the recommended way to grant AWS permissions to applications running on EKS.

data.title: Kubernetes Deployment YAML for EKS
data.content: A basic deployment manifest for an Nginx web server on EKS.
data.code:
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: nginx-deployment
  labels:
    app: nginx
spec:
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: nginx
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: nginx
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: nginx
        image: nginx:1.25
        ports:
        - containerPort: 80
        resources:
          requests:
            cpu: "100m"
            memory: "128Mi"
          limits:
            cpu: "250m"
            memory: "256Mi"
      serviceAccountName: my-app-sa
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: nginx-service
spec:
  selector:
    app: nginx
  ports:
    - port: 80
      targetPort: 80
  type: LoadBalancer

data.title: EKS vs ECS
data.text: EKS is more complex than ECS but is the standard Kubernetes platform. Choose ECS for simpler AWS-native container deployments. Choose EKS if you need Kubernetes portability or are already using Kubernetes tools.

terms.definition: The set of processes that control Kubernetes nodes and Pods (API server, scheduler, etcd). EKS manages this for you.
A group of EC2 instances managed by EKS that run your container workloads.
A rule that defines which Pods run on Fargate instead of EC2 nodes.
A method to assign IAM roles to Kubernetes service accounts for fine-grained AWS permissions.

data.title: Deploy an App to EKS
data.description: Create an EKS cluster using eksctl, deploy a sample app, and access it through a load balancer.
steps: Create an EKS cluster with a managed node group
Deploy the Nginx deployment and service YAML
Get the load balancer URL and open it in a browser
Scale the deployment to 5 replicas using kubectl
data.expectedOutcome: Your Nginx app is running on EKS and accessible via a load balancer URL.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: EKS is a managed Kubernetes control plane — AWS manages the control plane, you manage the nodes
Use kubectl to interact with EKS just like any other Kubernetes cluster
Fargate profiles let you run Pods without managing EC2 instances
IRSA is the recommended way to grant AWS permissions to EKS workloads
data.takeaway: EKS brings the full power of Kubernetes to AWS without the overhead of managing the control plane.
